title: Two-colour brioche
sourceNotes: Two-colour brioche is a technique that developed primarily in the late 20th and early 21st centuries. Description is original, derived from industry-standard brioche abbreviations per Craft Yarn Council. No direct PD source. sourceType: SYNTHESISED.

content.text: The secret of two-colour brioche is that the two colours are worked on alternating rows, never on the same row. Each colour takes exactly half the brioche cycle. A stitch that shows one colour on the right side shows the opposite colour on the reverse. The result is a fully reversible fabric where the colours simply swap sides. Each colour is carried up the edge rather than cut, so there are never more than two working yarns at once.
You need two balls of yarn in contrasting colours (referred to here as MC and CC), a pair of needles suited to the yarn weight, and a solid grounding in one-colour
brioche
. Cast on with MC.
Step by step
Abbreviations: brk1 = brioche knit; brp1 = brioche purl; sl1yo = slip 1 purlwise with yarn in front, then take yarn over needle.
Cast on an odd number of stitches with MC.
Set-up row with MC: *k1, sl1yo; repeat to last stitch, k1.
Join CC at the right edge. Row 1 (CC, right side): *sl1yo, brk1; repeat to last stitch, sl1yo. CC is now at the left edge; do not cut.
Row 2 (MC, right side): *brp1, sl1yo; repeat to last stitch, brp1. MC is now at the left edge. The two yarns alternate at each edge.
Row 3 (CC, wrong side): *sl1yo, brp1; repeat to last stitch, sl1yo.
Row 4 (MC, wrong side): *brk1, sl1yo; repeat to last stitch, brk1.
Repeat rows 1 to 4 for the fabric. Each four-row repeat is one full two-colour brioche cycle.
Where you'll see it

Two-colour brioche is used for scarves, cowls, and hat bodies where a reversible colourwork fabric is wanted. Because the two sides are mirror images in colour, no wrong side is visible when the scarf or cowl ends trail or fold outward. It has no direct ancestor in Victorian knitting manuals; the technique spread through the early 2000s knitting revival and is now widely taught.
Common faults
Working the wrong colour on the wrong row. Each colour must always work the same row in the 4-row cycle. Place a small safety pin of the corresponding colour on each yarn end as a reminder.
Yarn tangling at the edges. Because the yarns alternate at the edges, they will twist around each other after each pair of rows. Every two rows, swap the position of the two balls to undo the twist.

Dominant colour bleeding to the wrong side. In two-colour brioche, the MC should appear on one face and CC on the other. If both colours are visible on the same face, a yarn over was worked in the wrong colour, causing the brioche column to blend rather than separate.

What to try next: once the four-row cycle feels automatic, try shaping in brioche. Brioche increases use brkyobrk; decreases use brLsl dec or brRsl dec. These let you knit simple tapered cowls or hat shapes.
